t: Range XOR Queries with Subarray Reversals
o: We need point assignment, range XOR, and range reversal on an array of up to 1e5 with 1e5 queries. A segment tree cannot reverse lazily; the standard tool is an implicit treap (a balanced BST keyed by position) carrying a subtree XOR and a lazy reversal flag. Splitting at positions isolates any range in O(log n); XOR reads the isolated subtree's stored xor; reversal just swaps children lazily. Example 1: XOR of [2,3,4] is 5; after updating index 2 to 10 and reversing everything, XOR of the whole array is 5^4^10^2^1 = 8.
k: Implicit treap = balanced BST indexed by position, supporting split/merge in O(log n).
Store subtree XOR; reversal is a lazy child-swap since XOR is commutative and unaffected by order.
Point update = split out the single node, rewrite its value, merge back.

a.n: Approach 1: Implicit treap with lazy reversal
a.i: Each node stores value, subtree xor, size, heap priority, and a reversed flag. split(t, k) returns the first k nodes; merge concatenates. Push the reversal flag down before descending. Queries 1/2/3 each reduce to two splits and merges around the affected range.
s: Build the treap from the initial array by successive merges.
Type 2: split off [l, r], read its xor, merge back.
Type 3: split off [l, r], toggle its reversed flag, merge back.
Type 1: split off the single node at index, overwrite value and xor, merge back.
a.t: O((n + q) log n) — each split/merge is O(depth) on a randomized balanced treap

w: The observation that XOR is reversal-invariant is what makes lazy reversal a pure child swap — no data recomputation. Pitfalls: pushing the flag before every descent, recomputing size and xor on the way up, and splitting with correct length arithmetic (r - l + 1). Recursion depth is O(log n) expected, safe even in Python. Follow-up: add range assignment or range sum — both slot into the same pull/push framework.
